The cleaning and surface preparation process is akin to an electroplating line, which often take up a sizeable fraction of an electroplating shop’s floor space. An in-depth look at the individual steps used in cavity processing and cleanroom techniques is provided by Popielarski in a review presentation available on the Michigan State University website [6]. B.2.3 CAPEX Considerations The capital expenditures needed to accommodate the cleaning of high gradient accelerator structures are likely to be low relative to other costs in the fabrication process but can still be significant for a firm that does not already possess cleanroom capacity. A cleaning room may require significant building space, however, most laboratories or manufacturers with the capacity to produce high gradient accelerators will either already have a cleaning space or will have sufficient space to set up such a room. Additionally, a firm can partition a laboratory or workshop with a modular cleanroom. Compared to niobium superconducting cavities, the cavities used in high-gradient structures are likely much smaller, requiring smaller processing tanks (50 gal vs 150 gal) for electropolishing, degreasing, and rinsing. In this estimate, we assume a 50 gal tank size for all immersion processing steps. The requirements for a cleanroom and cleaning area can be estimated by prior experiences in optimizing a clean-room layout. As mentioned previously, Figure 14 shows an optimized layout of a clean-room area for processing high-gradient structures. This layout requires several assembly areas with varying classifications ranging from 100 to 10,000. Table 2 describes clean-room classifications as defined by particles per unit volume maintained in the cleanroom air, with lower classes having a stricter limit on the number of particles in air. These particle limits are maintained with high-flow filters and positive-pressure systems that keep out contaminants. Water used for chemistry tools, rinse tanks, and high-pressure rinsing should always be ultra-pure water (E-1, 18.1 MΩ-cm). This requires the installation of a fairly large ultra-pure water filtration system as well as a holding tank for re-filling rinse tanks in the cleanroom.
